analysis.one_liner: Requires colleges to report, prevent, and set fair procedures for campus sexual assault, dating violence, and stalking.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 43 cosponsors, including two Republicans, but was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and sent to a subcommittee in April 2013, where it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Higher Education Act to require every college receiving federal student aid to disclose statistics on domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault, and stalking; to run prevention and awareness programs for incoming students and new employees; to give victims written notice of their rights, confidentiality protections, and available services, whether or not they report the crime; and to follow minimum standards in campus disciplinary proceedings, including a preponderance-of-the-evidence standard and equal rights for the accuser and the accused. It also would have barred schools from retaliating against anyone who exercised these rights. The bill never left committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Students and employees at colleges that receive federal student aid — the vast majority of American higher education — would gain more accurate information about sexual violence at their schools, required prevention training, guaranteed confidentiality, and written notice of their rights and available services if they are victimized. Victims of campus sexual assault, dating violence, domestic violence, and stalking would get minimum protections in disciplinary proceedings: a prompt and impartial investigation by trained officials, a preponderance-of-the-evidence standard, an advisor of their choice, and written notice of outcomes and appeal rights for both sides.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Students and campus sexual assault victims

how_it_helps.text: Required colleges to publish statistics on domestic violence, dating violence, and stalking incidents reported to campus security or local police, so students could see how often these offenses occur at their school.

Required every college to run prevention and awareness programs for all incoming students and new employees, covering the definition of consent, how to recognize warning signs of abuse, and safe options for bystanders to intervene.

Guaranteed victims a written explanation of their rights — including counseling, victim advocacy, and legal services on campus and in the community, and help changing their academic, living, transportation, or working arrangements — whether or not they report the crime to police.

Set minimum rules for campus disciplinary proceedings: a prompt, fair, and impartial investigation by officials trained on these offenses, the preponderance-of-the-evidence standard, and equal rights for the accuser and the accused to have an advisor of their choice present and to be told the outcome and appeal options in writing.

Required colleges to protect victim confidentiality in public recordkeeping and in timely warnings, and banned school employees from retaliating against anyone for exercising their rights under the law.

analysis.who_pays: Colleges and universities would bear the cost of compiling new statistics, running prevention programs for every incoming class, training disciplinary officials, and meeting the new procedural standards, with no dedicated federal funding attached. Schools also lose discretion over how they handle campus disciplinary proceedings, which must meet the bill's minimum standards.

drawbacks.text: The bill required campus disciplinary proceedings to use the 'preponderance of the evidence' standard — the lowest standard in American law — a choice that drew sustained criticism on due-process grounds because accused students could be found responsible and expelled on a bare majority of the evidence, with serious consequences for their records and prospects.

The bill imposed new duties on colleges — annual awareness programs for all incoming students and employees, trained investigators, written victim notifications, and expanded crime statistics — without any dedicated funding to pay for them, which smaller institutions said would fall hardest on their budgets.

Expanded statistical reporting on dating violence, domestic violence, and stalking, which are often unreported and hard to categorize, risked producing numbers that vary widely campus to campus and are difficult to compare.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete and largely one-sided: the bill required schools to tell students what happened, teach prevention, protect victim confidentiality, and guarantee accuser and accused equal rights in campus proceedings, at modest cost. The costs fall on colleges and universities, which would face new reporting, training, and disciplinary-procedure requirements without dedicated funding, and the bill's choice of the preponderance-of-the-evidence standard for campus proceedings was contested on due-process grounds. On balance the bill's benefits to student safety and transparency outweighed its compliance costs, and Congress chose not to take them up.

outcome.mechanism: The House bill was sent to the Education and the Workforce Committee and then to its higher education subcommittee, and no one ever scheduled a hearing or a vote, so it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 25, 2013 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
On April 23, 2013 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Higher Education and Workforce Training — the last action ever taken on it.
It carried 43 cosponsors, 41 Democrats and 2 Republicans, but the committee never scheduled a markup or a vote before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Colleges and universities are better off: they face none of the new reporting, prevention, and disciplinary-procedure requirements the bill would have imposed, and no public statistics on domestic violence, dating violence, or stalking at their schools.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Colleges avoiding new reporting and disciplinary mandates

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily but not entirely Democratic — 41 of 43 cosponsors were Democrats — and the bill never reached a vote, so no one's actual position was recorded on the floor; the deciding fact was that the Republican-run committee never scheduled action.

industries.note: The bill imposed new compliance duties on every institution receiving federal student aid: publishing statistics on domestic violence, dating violence, and stalking; running prevention programs for all incoming students and employees; protecting victim confidentiality; and meeting minimum standards for campus disciplinary proceedings, including the preponderance-of-the-evidence standard. It carried no funding, so schools would have absorbed the cost, along with greater public visibility into how often these offenses occur on their campuses.

Victims on and around campuses stood to gain written notice of their rights, access to counseling and advocacy services, confidentiality protections, and enforceable minimum standards in campus disciplinary proceedings. They are people rather than an industry, but they are the group the bill's benefits were designed to reach.
